title: Anchoring

scenes.text: A random wheel changed what people *believed*.
scenes.vo: Scientists spun a rigged wheel of fortune, and it changed what people believed was true.
In 1974, Tversky and Kahneman had people spin a wheel that stopped on either 10 or 65.

scenes.text: Then: what % of UN countries are African?
scenes.vo: Then they asked: what percentage of countries in the United Nations are African?
People who saw 10 guessed 25 percent, on average.
People who saw 65 guessed 45 percent. A meaningless number dragged their answer up.
This is anchoring. The first number you see becomes the reference point for everything after it.
It's why shops show a crossed-out price, and why the first number in a salary negotiation matters so much.

scenes.text: Drop the anchor *first*, or decide your number before you look.
scenes.vo: So drop the anchor first, or decide your number before you look at theirs.

caption:
The first number you see quietly rewrites every number after it. ⚓ Even when it comes from a spinning wheel.

Where have you been anchored? Sales, salary, rent? 👇
source: Tversky, A. & Kahneman, D. (1974). Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases. Science, 185(4157).
